newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Poll shows confidence in Czech PM low but stable.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows confidence in Czech PM low but stable.

text.p: Public confidence in Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, in decline since January, appears to have steadied but remains at an all-time low of 31 percent of those questioned, an opinion poll released on Wednesday showed.
The survey, carried out among 1,601 respondents aged 18 and over by private pollster STEM during the first week of July, turned up a percentage unchanged from a similar survey in June.
After the 1989 revolution which ousted the Communist government, Klaus won acclaim for quickly introducing a voucher-based privatisation scheme which put thousands of firms into private hands.

But the economy, once considered a model of reform, has been hit recently by a huge trade deficit blamed largely on poor corporate restructuring. That led to fierce speculative attacks on the value of the crown, forcing the central bank to float the currency on May 27 and watch it fall further.

Klaus narrowly averted being ousted at the beginning of June, cutting a last-minute deal with an independent deputy to squeak through a confidence vote on his three-party coalition and its package of tough austerity measures by 101-99 in the lower house of parliament.
As economic problems grew, bringing to light many of the stumbling blocks the fledgling economy still has to face up to, Klaus's poll rating declined from 51 percent in January to its current level.

But Klaus's foil on the Czech political scene, President Vaclav Havel, who acts more as a philosophical balancing wheel for the country than a political leader, maintains the broad trust which brought him to power after the revolution.

The STEM survey showed that confidence in the former dissident playwright turned president, who is often at odds with the right-wing Klaus's espousal of individualism in society, remains solid at 66 percent.

Havel, who is not a member of any political party. is elected by parliament and is not directly involved in party politics. He has said he will stand again in the spring of next year and political analysts believe he will face little in the way of opposition.
The next parliamentary elections are not due until June, 2000, but the analysts believe an early poll might be forced by autumn next year.
